evidence.quote: (due to T. Kosciumaka, J. Radoszewski, W. Rytter and T. Waleń [43]): A word of length n contains Theta(n√n) inequivalent abelian-squares. Author: Michaël Rao [66]. Erdös formulated two fundamental problems: (1) (1957,1961): Is there arbitrarily long abelian-square-free words over a finite alphabet? (2) (1961): Is it possible to avoid long squares over a binary alphabet? R.C. Entringer, D.E. Jackson and J.A. Schatz gave a positive answer to the second question [25]. In 2002 Mäkelä put similar questions with regards to the abelian squares or cubes over binary or ternary alphabets [51]. In his talk at WORDS 2015, Rao presented technics for deciding whether a morphic word avoids abelian and k-abelian repetitions: in particular, this allowed him to prove that long abelian squares are avoidable over a ternary alphabet. artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in \Sigma^*$ be a word of length $n$. A factor (contiguous subword) of the form $uv$ with $|u|=|v|$ is called an abelian square if $v$ is a permutation of $u$, i.e. for every letter $a \in \Sigma$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $a$ in $v$. Two abelian squares $u_1 v_1$ and $u_2 v_2$ (occurring as factors of $w$) are called equivalent if $|u_1|=|u_2|$ and $u_1$ is a permutation of $u_2$ (equivalently they have the same length and the same Parikh vector on each half); otherwise they are called inequivalent. Let $A(w)$ denote the number of pairwise inequivalent abelian squares occurring as factors of $w$, and define
$$ A(n) \; = \; \max_{|w|=n} A(w). $$
Prove or disprove: $A(n) = \Theta(n\sqrt{n})$, i.e. there exist constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$ c_1\, n\sqrt{n} \;\le\; A(n) \;\le\; c_2\, n\sqrt{n}. $$
artifact.status_search_result: The conjectured Θ(n√n) bound on the maximum number of pairwise inequivalent abelian squares in a word of length n is stated as a conjecture by Kociumaka, Radoszewski, Rytter and Waleń. Their work establishes a lower bound Ω(n^{1.5}/log n) (over a binary alphabet) but the matching upper bound O(n√n) is, to current public knowledge, not established; subsequent works on abelian-square-rich words and related extremal questions also do not appear to have closed the gap. The problem appears to remain open with partial bounds.

status_evidence.title: Words with the Maximum Number of Abelian Squares
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses extremal numbers of abelian-square factors in words, with related upper/lower bounds.
status_evidence.claim: Related extremal results on abelian squares; the inequivalent-count problem remains a conjecture.

status_evidence.title: Abelian-Square-Rich Words
status_evidence.snippet: Constructs words containing many abelian squares, related to the conjectured Θ(n√n) growth.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work studies abelian-square-rich words but does not establish the matching upper bound.
